title: Ar-Raqib, the Watchful
tomorrow: Jordan's grandma is praying for Amira. is that like du'a?

cards: A message box with a whole paragraph in it, and a thumb hovering over send. The finalist list for Amira's scholarship went up this morning, and Kayla is on it too.

Now the group chat is picking Kayla apart, and Amira has typed the one story nobody else knows: the venue deposit Kayla forgot, the one Amira quietly fixed. Every word of it is true. The chat would love it.
Before she decides, the Qur'an has something to say about that hover, about the second between typing and sending.

teach.h: AN OBSERVER READY FOR EVERY WORD.
teach.b: Surah Qaf says of each person: "He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready." The Arabic word for that watcher is raqib, and today's Name is Ar-Raqib, the Watchful.

teach.h: WATCHING OVER YOU, FOR YOUR SAKE.
teach.b: Allah's own watching comes at the very start of Surah An-Nisa: "Lo! Allah hath been a Watcher over you." That can sound like a camera in the ceiling.

But look where the verse puts it: right after a line about caring for the family ties that bind you. The Watchful watches over you, the way a parent watches a toddler near the stairs. Close attention, for your sake.

For the tongue, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave one clean test, in Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them speak good or keep silent. Notice what the test is not.
It isn't, is it true? A story can be true and still not good. And a fault you once covered stays covered.
So the hover over send isn't weakness. It's the exact moment the test happens. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.
Muslim teachers took this Name and made a practice of it, called muraqaba: keeping watch over your own heart, because you know you're seen.
For three seconds before send, you can be your own raqib.

how: Muslims learn the hadith 'speak good or keep silent' (Sahih al-Bukhari) as a rule for speech; muraqaba, watching over one's own heart because Allah sees, is a practice taught especially in Sufi circles.

o: the one who punishes every harsh word
the guard who stands at the gates of heaven
the Watchful, who watches over you closely

p: an observer ready for every word

s: Ar-Raqib is mainly about God catching you out
4:1 puts the watching right after care for family ties: close attention, for your sake.
the hadith's test for speech is 'is it true?'
it's 'speak good or keep silent' (Sahih al-Bukhari). true and good aren't the same test.
Surah Qaf says no word is spoken without an observer ready
"He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready" (50:18, Pickthall).

games.q: your aunt asks what you really think of your cousin's new fiancé. you have an answer that's true and cutting. what fits today's Name?
o: say what's good and true about him, and leave the cutting part unsaid.
say all of it. honesty is what God is watching for.
say nothing now, then tell her the cutting part later in private.
games.why: the hadith asks for good speech or silence. truth isn't the only test; the second option is the skimmer's version, and the third just moves the cut to later.

practice: Choose one conversation coming up today: a group chat, dinner, a call. Name what you hope to say in it, and then the one line you're tempted to add that isn't good.

Decide now what you'll do when that line rises: a breath, a pause, three seconds before send. If it helps, picture the send button, and your thumb resting beside it, not on it. Then let the sit be the pause itself.

wordCard.voice: Ar-Raqib. The Watchful, close as an observer at your shoulder, watching over you for your sake. Name forty-three.

orig.note: Arabic: the Watchful. 50:18 uses the same word for the observer at every word; 4:1 uses it for Allah.

carryVoice: The line to keep: watched, and the hover between good words and quiet is where it's decided. That's day ninety-one.
